Acceptance summary:

The manuscript addresses the ability of copepods to find mates in a turbulent environment, a major question in marine science. Through comprehensive experiments and models the authors demonstrate that mating occurs despite turbulence and that turbulence facilitates encounters. Animals are brought close to one another by the underlying flow; when a male perceives a potential mate, it achieves contact by direct and vigorous swimming. Perception occurs within 4 mm from the potential mate, and, intriguingly, this range is similar in calm and turbulent environments, suggesting copepods sensory systems are insensitive to turbulence.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your work entitled "Efficient mate finding in planktonic copepods swimming in turbulence" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and a Senior Editor. The reviewers have opted to remain anonymous.

The manuscript addresses the ability of copepods to find mates in a turbulent environment, a major question in marine science. The authors investigate the encounter rates by experimentally monitoring alive and dead copepods in a turbulent flow and model their individual trajectories. These are interesting data and a robust modelling methodology which merits publication, however we find that the level of biological insight provided by this work is not sufficient to grant publication in eLife. There is a long literature about encounter rates of copepods in turbulent environment, including by these authors, and the overall picture is largely consistent with the author's findings. The main novelty of the present manuscript is the focus on mating.

However, the authors do not currently monitor actual mating events.

Documenting mating is especially important because it is not clear whether these animals do mate at such high turbulence intensity. In fact, trace following behavior by males suggests these animals may be adapted to mate at low turbulence levels (although this remains to be proven).

If the authors were able to distinguish males from females, the experiments may be adapted to documenting the actual mating between individuals. We would welcome such a study that fills a void in current knowledge, and would consider it as a new submission as this entirely changes the focus of the manuscript.

Reviewer #1:

This manuscript addresses an important aspect of marine science. Copepods are the most abundant metazoan on the planet and play an important role in recycling organic matter and in passing organic matter to higher trophic levels. The aim of this paper was to model the encounter rates of copepods in a turbulent environment and test the model by observing the interaction of copepods (Eurytemora affinis) in a turbulent field.

I have several fundamental issues with the manuscript that makes it not publishable in its current form. There are some small copy editing aspects that will also need to be addressed. I did not list them here since I assume the manuscript will be rewritten.

The theoretical approach is not novel. Gerritsen and Stickler (1977) modeled encounter rates of copepod based on their relative swimming speeds. Osborn and Rothshild, 1988 added turbulence to the equation. Since then (nearly 30 years ago) there have been updates to the models including the effects of turbulence on the perceptive field. Most study have assumed a parabolic shape of encounter success with increased turbulence. The initial rise in the encounter rate is due to the added relative velocity due to turbulence. The decrease in successful encounter at high turbulence is driven initially by the decrease in perception distance and then, at very high turbulence levels, by the inability of the copepods to react to each other within the short time frame of the encounter. The model shown in this study does not appear to advance our current understanding of how turbulence may enhance or diminish mating in copepods.

The authors state that " We study this important yet unexplored aspect of plankton ecology in the context of mating and show that self-locomotion creates large differences in the inward component of the pairwise radial relative velocity of copepods, which directly results in larger encounter rates at separation distances comparable to the spatial extend (this should be extent) of the flow field they generate while swimming (Kiorboe et al., 2014)"

This is simply not true. There is a rich history in the literature of looking at the effects of turbulence on the encounter rate of copepods. While not all of the work deals specifically with mating, it is described as encounter rate, or capture volume as the authors have done in this study.

In terms of the biological experiments in which copepods were observed and tracked in a turbulent regime, I have 2 suggestions that would make this manuscript stronger.

1) It would be valuable to quantify the ability of male copepods to actually grab and mate with female copepods under different levels of turbulence. Currently based on Figures 1-4 it is unclear if males and females were individually identified. This is important because females don't track males or other females. Only the males do the mate tracking. It also remains unclear if the males actually grabbed on to the females and mated or did they just get close to each other in the video? If the authors can identify the females and males in the video (using swimming patterns), the number of successful mating events could be quantified. This would be valuable data.

2) I am concerned about the level of turbulence used in this study. The copepods used in this study are on the order of 1.2 mm. The Kolmogorov length scale used in this study was 0.450 mm. The time scale was 0.2s. These turbulence levels are extremely high – not just at the high end of ocean turbulence. These levels are on the order of a tidal bore. The supplementary figure (Appendix 1—figure 3) shows a male copepod tracking a female's chemical trail. This mate tracking behavior suggests that these copepods are evolved to mate in relatively quiet waters. The length scales shown in this figure define a volume of 100 mls. At the turbulence levels used in this study, the eddy size would be 0.0453 cm3 or 0.091 nanoliters. This is a tiny volume. At this level the trails laid by the female would be destroyed. The experiments need to be done at more moderate levels of turbulence to be realistic for this species.

Finally as a closing comment – the capture volume of copepods in turbulence is linearly related to the swimming speed of the copepods and the added speed caused by turbulence (Rothschild and Osborn). However the encounter rate is exponentially related to the perceptive distance. This has a huge impact of the ability of copepods to find each other. Currently, not much is known about the effects of turbulence on the mechano-receptive or chemo-receptive abilities of copepods. However it is likely that they are impacted by turbulence. Since the encounter rate is so highly dependent on this parameter is difficult to model the outcome without a kernel that parameterizes it impact.

Reviewer #2:

This is an interesting paper dealing with the ability of calanoid copepods to find mates in a turbulent environment. The study is based on a combination of analytical models and careful experimental studies. It is found that copepods have an enhanced encounter rate in turbulent environments compared to than in calm waters. The conclusion is consistent with a number of related investigations dealing with encounters in turbulence. The topic of the study is thus not entire new, but the methods and results are well described and add to the existing knowledge in the field. As far as I can see, the paper is giving adequate credit to previous studies. I can, in principle, recommend publication of the paper, but have some comments for the authors. Some need their attention, and some I think should be considered.

1) Figure 1 needs attention. The caption mentions some cones, that I do not find, please clarify. The figure contains "blur" in blue colour: I presume this should represent turbulence? It is not explained. In part due to this blue colour, the colour coding of the trajectories becomes unclear: I had to enlarge the figure significantly to see this. Of course any reader can do the same, but only in the electronic version. The figure is important in my opinion, so it deserves more attention. Figure 1C has interesting information, this comes out quite clearly.

2) The authors discuss finite inertia of the copepods (an entire section is devoted to this) but not much their finite size which is mentioned only in bypassing, e.g. caption of Appendix 1—figure 1. It seems to me that organisms are discussed as being point particles. The mass density of copepods is not much different from that of water, after all, but the finite size can be important and have been discussed in the literature. Finite size effects may not be dramatic for spherical particles, but elongated ones are likely to cluster in turbulent flows (this is actually consistent with results given by the black symbols for dead copepods in Figure 4). The authors refer to comparisons of measurements for dead and live copepods, but it is not clear how they make use of this information. I agree though that the finite-size information is present in this measurement.

3) I would have expected the elongation of pheromone traces due to turbulence to be important. Indeed, it is mentioned in the Introduction. Since the flow is incompressible, the volume of a trace is constant, and since it elongates (nearly exponentially, e.g. Batchelor, "The effect of homogeneous turbulence on material lines and surfaces", Proc. R. Soc. London, Ser. A 213, 349 (1952)) it must thin out quite rapidly and some places be too thin to be detectable. The pheromone traces will in reality break-up into several smaller ones. I would have expected discussions like this to take more place. The authors might consider the point?

4) As far as I can see, it is assumed that copepods will encounter as soon as they enter within a suitably defined "region of interaction", this is how I read the discussion of Figure 1B, for instance. MacKenzie et al.,. "Evidence for a dome-shaped relationship between turbulence and larval fish ingestion rates", Limnol. Oceanogr. 39, 1790 (1994) have argued that even in case two organisms come within a contact range, it might still happen that turbulent motions separate them again to reduce the probability of an ultimate encounter. It seems that this model has found some support (Pecseli et al. "Feeding of plankton in turbulent oceans and lakes", Limnol. Oceanogr. 64, 1034 (2019)). Can this scenario have some bearing for the authors problem?

5) Finally, although the disposition of the paper is good, it is at places difficult to read (at least for me). Some sentences can be very long, often over 3 or more lines of text. It might be advisable to go through the manuscript once more and break up such long sentences.

Reviewer #3:

This paper reports on a study on the encounter dynamics of planktonic copepods in turbulent flows. It presents state-of-the-art measurements on the simultaneous tracking of copepods and fluid tracers in turbulence, which allow to assess the approaching velocity of copepods pairs down to a scale of 1mm (approximately one body length). The average properties of the approaching process are interpreted by means of an empirical statistical model. The conclusions drawn from the study, and in particular their biological implications on the efficiency of mate finding, are in my view not sufficiently supported by the experimental evidence, as the actual mating events are not measured experimentally.

Here below, my three main remarks on this study:

1) The paper contains new measurements and a number of interesting and solid results on the mechanistic (physical) aspects of copepod dynamics. The measurements reported in Figure 2 convey in a convincing way the message that the active motion of copepods boosts their approach.

2) One main limitation of the experimental technique is the inability to detect effective contact among copepods. This limitation makes the biological considerations about mating rather speculative.

3) The probabilistic model of plankton motion at difference from previously existing models neglects the existence of correlations between the swimming behavior (cruising, jumping) and turbulent cues (strain, shear or rotation dominated events). This is a central question to which many studies have been devoted in the past. Can this assumption be tested against the experimental data? In the preset setup the simultaneous tracking of copepods and fluid tracers could in principle allow to characterize the turbulence in the vicinity of a copepod.

In the light of the limitation at point 2), I judge the article not suitable for publication in eLife. However, the authors shall be definitely encouraged to publish this work in a different form.

results.result: Zooplankton, particularly calanoid copepods, play pivotal ecological roles by channeling nutrients and energy through trophic levels, supporting fish development, contributing to the biological carbon pump, and dominating metazoan biomass in marine and estuarine environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C1–C3, C19–C20 establish the ecological importance of zooplankton and copepods through multiple citations to established literature (Cushing 1975, Beaugrand et al. 2003, Steinberg and Landry 2017). These are well-established facts in marine ecology supported by prior work.

results.result: Motility in zooplankton enables navigation, resource exploitation, inter-organism interactions, and mediates processes determining individual fitness and ecosystem dynamics at multiple scales.
results.evaluation: Claims C4–C8 describe the functional importance of motility, supported by multiple citations (Genin et al. 2005, Menden-Deuer and Grünbaum 2006, Bagøien and Kiørboe 2005, Kiørboe et al. 2009, Gemmell et al. 2012, Kiørboe 2008, 2011). These represent established knowledge about zooplankton behavior.

results.result: Turbulence in marine environments imposes physical constraints on zooplankton locomotion and may interfere with fundamental behavioral processes, yet the nature and importance of these interactions remain poorly understood due to technical challenges and lack of validated models.
results.evaluation: Claims C9–C18 establish the research gap and motivation. These are supported by citations (McManus and Woodson 2012, Michalec et al. 2015a, Incze et al. 2001, Visser et al. 2009, Yen et al. 2008, Rothschild and Osborn 1988, Pécseli et al. 2010) and represent the state of knowledge prior to this study.

results.result: In calm water, calanoid copepods use pheromone trails for mate finding, but turbulence disrupts these chemical signals through exponential elongation, thinning, fragmentation, and diffusion, rendering them undetectable within seconds.
results.evaluation: Claims C21–C28 describe pheromone-based mating strategies and their disruption by turbulence. Supported by citations (Katona 1973, Doall et al. 1998, Yen et al. 1998, Bagøien and Kiørboe 2005, Batchelor 1952, Shraiman and Siggia 2000, Kiørboe et al. 2005) and physical principles of turbulent mixing.

results.result: Sexual dimorphism in swimming patterns (convoluted female trajectories vs. persistent male trajectories) increases mating probability in calm water but disappears in turbulence, leaving the mechanisms of mate finding in flowing environments unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C29–C33 describe behavioral strategies in calm water and their failure in turbulence. Supported by citations (Kiørboe and Bagøien 2005, Michalec et al. 2015a, Visser and Kiørboe 2006) and logical inference about turbulent redistribution.

results.result: Copepods achieve high encounter rates in turbulence through combined turbulent advection and active swimming, then males convert encounters to contacts via directed motion within a ~4mm perception radius, maintaining this ability even in strong turbulence and leading to successful mating.
results.evaluation: Claims C34–C41, C45, C85–C86, C91, C108–C116, C119 describe the core experimental findings. Supported by experimental data (Figures 1–4), showing encounter rates, directed motion, perception distance, and mating events. The observations are internally consistent and demonstrate the two-step mechanism (enhanced encounters + directed pursuit).

results.result: Active swimming via frequent relocation jumps, rather than passive turbulent advection, is the primary mechanism driving high encounter rates in copepods, with living copepods departing more from flow streamlines than dead ones and achieving velocities exceeding typical turbulent velocities.
results.evaluation: Claims C60–C61, C67, C75–C77, C160–C161, C165, C169 establish the importance of active motion. Supported by experimental data (Figures 1–2, Appendix 1-figure 1) showing clearance rate ratios >1 and trajectory departures. Citation to Michalec et al. 2017 provides prior evidence for jumping behavior.

results.result: Males exhibit directed motion toward conspecifics within a ~4mm perception radius (corresponding to hydrodynamic signal detection range), with this behavior occurring at similar distances in calm water and turbulence, revealing copepods' ability to distinguish conspecific signals from turbulent noise within the viscous subrange.
results.evaluation: Claims C80, C89, C94–C98, C103, C105, C107, C162 describe the perception and pursuit mechanism. Supported by experimental data (Figure 3) showing negative mean radial velocities at short separations, and citations (Bagøien and Kiørboe 2005, Doall et al. 1998, Yen et al. 1998, Ting and Snell 2003). The similar perception distance in calm and turbulent conditions is a key novel finding.

results.result: Inertial effects due to copepod density, size, and shape do not result in substantial preferential concentration at organism scales, reducing the geometric collision kernel to the clearance rate component.
results.evaluation: Claims C47–C49, C130–C131 describe the absence of preferential concentration. Supported by experimental data (Figure 5) showing correlation functions near unity, and citation to Fiabane et al. 2012 confirming similar findings for neutrally buoyant particles. This is an important negative result.

results.result: Preferential concentration in turbulence can substantially increase encounter rates for particles with different density or finite size, driven by small-scale eddies causing clustering in strain-dominated (heavy particles) or vorticity-dominated (light particles) regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C120–C126 provide background on preferential concentration. Supported by citations (Reade and Collins 2000, Sundaram and Collins 1997, Guala et al. 2008, Fouxon 2012, Tagawa et al. 2012, Schmitt and Seuront 2008). This is established knowledge providing context for the negative result in copepods.

results.result: Behavioral clustering occurs at small scales (<3mm) due to inward motion within the perception radius, with enhanced clustering at larger scales in calm water likely involving pheromone trail communication.
results.evaluation: Claims C133–C134, C136–C137 describe behavioral clustering. Supported by experimental data (Figure 5) showing elevated correlation at short separations, and citations (Katona 1973, Appendix 1-figure 3) documenting pheromone tracking. The mechanism at larger scales involves speculation but is supported by observational evidence.

results.result: A semi-empirical model accurately predicts encounter rates by superposing turbulent velocity and independent organism motion, requiring only the probability density function of organism velocity in calm water and avoiding simplifying assumptions about movement patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C142–C144, C149–C150, C152–C154, C186–C188, C192–C193 describe the model. The model shows satisfactory agreement with data (estimated γ=1.2 cm³/s vs measured 1.6 cm³/s at r=4mm). The approach is validated experimentally and represents a methodological advance over previous models requiring free parameters.

results.result: The experimental turbulence parameters (velocity 5.6 mm/s, integral length 6mm, Kolmogorov scales 0.2s and 0.45mm, energy dissipation 3×10⁻⁵ m²/s³) are comparable to field conditions in coastal areas and estuaries where E. affinis lives.
results.evaluation: Claims C51–C54, C57–C58 describe experimental conditions. Supported by Table 1 data and citations (Yamazaki and Squires 1996, Yen et al. 2008, Pécseli et al. 2019). The parameters are well-characterized and appropriate for the study objectives.

results.result: Encounters are defined as events where copepod centroids are separated by <1mm (approximately one body length), meaning observed encounters represent actual collisions/contacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C62–C65 define the encounter criterion. This is an explicit methodological definition supported by knowledge of organism size and the experimental resolution. The definition is appropriate for studying contact events.

results.result: Encounter rates in turbulence are comparable to or exceed those in calm water, but passive transport alone does not increase rates beyond calm-water motility—active swimming is required to achieve high encounter rates.
results.evaluation: Claims C164, C168, C170 compare encounter rates across conditions. Supported by experimental data (Figure 2B) showing clearance rate ratios. Citations (Rothschild and Osborn 1988, Visser et al. 2009, MacKenzie et al. 1994, Lewis and Pedley 2000) provide theoretical context.

results.result: Contrary to assumptions that turbulence reduces successful encounters due to decreased perception and reaction time, copepods maintain efficient mating in turbulence, suggesting reproduction is not restricted to calm conditions and relaxing boundaries between quiescent and turbulent environments for fitness.
results.evaluation: Claims C42–C44, C171–C174, C176 contrast findings with prior assumptions. Supported by experimental data showing successful mating in turbulence and citations (MacKenzie et al. 1994, Kiørboe and MacKenzie 1995, MacKenzie and Kiørboe 2000, Pécseli et al. 2019) documenting the prior paradigm. This represents a significant conceptual advance.

results.result: Copepods increase swimming activity in turbulence through more frequent relocation jumps reaching velocities exceeding turbulent velocities, potentially allowing them to depart from flow streamlines, achieve directed motion, and retain fitness advantages of motility.
results.evaluation: Claims C156–C159 describe behavioral adaptation to turbulence. C156–C157 are supported by citation to Michalec et al. 2017 and Yamazaki and Squires 1996. C158–C159 involve speculation about functional significance but are supported by citation to Genin et al. 2005 and the experimental results.

results.result: Previous models of plankton encounter rates face challenges from flow-behavior coupling and limited empirical validation, with early models superposing squared velocity differences and later improvements considering flow correlation and perception capabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C177–C184 review prior modeling approaches. Supported by citations (Boffetta et al. 2006, Pécseli et al. 2010, Ardeshiri et al. 2017, Rothschild and Osborn 1988, Gerritsen and Strickler 1977, Kiørboe and MacKenzie 1995, Lewis and Pedley 2000, Pécseli et al. 2014, MacKenzie et al. 1994, Lewis and Pedley 2001, Lewis 2003, Visser et al. 2009, Pécseli et al. 2019). results.result: Zooplankton can sense and respond to hydrodynamic forces by modulating swimming activity and velocity, meaning their interactions with turbulence include active behavioral responses in addition to physical effects.
